paragraphs.source_en: The little one was making a wild commotion; when she flicked her chopsticks upward, Tonko had just finished serving herself rice. Tonko, as befitted an elder sister, could not look on and ignore the jumble on her younger sister’s face, so she said, “Oh! Little one, this is terrible; your face is covered with grains of rice.” As she said this, she at once set about cleaning her sister’s face. First she removed the grain of rice that had taken lodgings on her sister’s nose. Do you suppose she threw away the grain she had removed? Not at all; she immediately put it into her own mouth, which astonished me. Next she began clearing her sister’s cheeks, where the grains had gathered in clusters; by count there must have been twenty or so on the two sides together. The elder sister carefully picked them off one by one and ate them, until at last she had eaten every grain from her younger sister’s face. At that moment, Sunko, who until then had been quietly chewing pickles, suddenly scooped several bits of sweet potato from the freshly served miso soup and thrust them into her mouth all at once. You gentlemen surely know that nothing scalds the mouth quite like hot sweet potato fished out of soup. Even an adult, if not careful, will feel as though he has been burned and cry out. How much more, then, would someone like Sunko, with no experience of sweet potatoes, naturally be thrown into confusion. Sunko cried “Wah!” and spat the sweet potato from her mouth onto the dining table. Somehow two or three of those pieces slid right in front of the little one and stopped just where she could conveniently reach them. The little one had always been fond of sweet potatoes, and when her favorite food suddenly appeared before her eyes, she promptly threw down her chopsticks, grabbed it by hand, and devoured it all.

paragraphs.source_en: The master, who had been watching this spectacle from the start, said not a word and devoted himself solely to eating his own rice. By now he had already finished his soup and was in the midst of using a toothpick. It appears that, in the matter of educating his children, the master has adopted an absolutely laissez-faire policy. In time, even if all three daughters became some sort of Russet Shikibu or Mouse-gray Shikibu, each taking a lover and eloping hand in hand, their father would likely remain unconcerned, still eating his rice and drinking his soup as before. He may truly be called a man of no action at all. Yet when I observe those in present society who are said to be men of action, they know nothing beyond lying to lure people in, getting ahead of others to cheat them first, putting on a show of strength to intimidate them, and setting traps to ruin them. Even the youths in middle schools imitate these people step for step, mistakenly thinking they cannot make themselves felt otherwise, proudly doing what they ought by rights to blush over, and regarding themselves as future gentlemen. One cannot say that the action of such people is unreal; it is simply the skill of a rogue. I, too, am a Japanese cat, and so I possess some small measure of patriotism. Whenever I see these so-called men of action, I feel like giving them a thrashing. For every additional person of this kind, the nation declines by just that much. A school that cultivates such students is a disgrace to the school. A nation made up of such people is a disgrace to the nation. I simply cannot understand why, though it is plainly a disgrace, society is full of such things. It seems that the humans living in Japan have not even the spirit of a cat like me; it is disheartening indeed. Compared with such rogue-style men of action, my master must be called a far superior sort of person. His lack of spirit, his incompetence, his refusal to play tricks or show petty cleverness: these are precisely the proofs of his superiority.

paragraphs.source_en: Having finished this inactive yet peaceful breakfast, the master soon put on his Western clothes, got into a rickshaw, and at last presented himself at the Nihonzutsumi police substation. As he was leaving the house, the master asked the rickshaw man, “Do you know the place called Nihonzutsumi?” The rickshaw man merely laughed, heh-heh. The master even took pains to impress upon him, “I mean Nihonzutsumi near Yoshiwara, where the pleasure quarter is.” It was quite comical.
